name: Polynesian Languages (Genus Template)

formality.description: Polynesian languages express formality through vocabulary choice, discourse particles, and speech style rather than pronominal T-V systems. Many have distinct ceremonial/oratorial registers for formal occasions.

gender.inclusiveGuidance: Polynesian languages have no grammatical gender. Pronouns are gender-neutral.

linguisticChallenges.particleSystem: Polynesian languages rely heavily on particles (tense/aspect markers, case markers, prepositions) rather than inflectional morphology. Word boundaries and particle placement are critical for meaning but difficult for MT to learn from limited data.
linguisticChallenges.limitedConsonantInventory: Most Polynesian languages have very small consonant inventories (8-15 consonants) and strict CV syllable structure. This creates many near-homophones distinguished only by vowel length (macrons/glottal stops), making diacritical accuracy critical.
linguisticChallenges.diacriticalSensitivity: Macrons (ā, ē, ī, ō, ū) and glottal stops (ʻ) are phonemic — they distinguish words with completely different meanings. Most MT systems strip or ignore these diacritics, producing ambiguous or incorrect output.
linguisticChallenges.culturalEmbedding: Many words carry deep cultural/spiritual meaning that cannot be directly translated. Neologisms for modern concepts must be carefully coined to avoid cultural inappropriateness.

contactInfluences.notes: Colonial and post-colonial English dominance across Polynesia. All Polynesian languages are in various stages of revitalization.

notes: Genus template for Polynesian languages (Māori, Hawaiian, Samoan, Tongan, Tahitian, etc.). All share particle-heavy syntax, limited consonant inventories, and critical diacritical sensitivity.
